body:
Looks like you are hitting the instance shader uniform limit. This is a limit set by hardware. Older NVidia devices only support 4096 items total. Each sprite using instance uniforms allocates an array of 16 uniforms, so you can only have up to 256 Sprites on your devices that use per-instance uniforms.

AMD devices typically support up to 262,144 items (16384 sprites), so it takes a lot longer to hit the limit. 

These are hardware limits unfortunately, so you need to work around them

Are you saying that the max buffer size on an integrated AMD graphics card is larger than the max buffer size on an RTX 2070 S? The RTX Super released in 2019 and has 8 GB of VRAM. The Ryzen 5 5600G released in 2021 has a couple of L caches less than 16 MB, with the rest of the memory being shared with the system RAM.

Also, what do you mean by "items"? Some uniforms like dmat4x4 can be as big as 128 bytes, while a float is only 4 bytes.

> Are you saying that the max buffer size on an integrated AMD graphics card is larger than the max buffer size on an RTX 2070 S? 

Yes. It's not about how powerful the device is. AMD often chooses to allow much bigger buffers while NVidia often chooses to give the bare minimum size.

> Also, what do you mean by "items"? Some uniforms like mat4x4 can be as big as 128 bytes, while a float is only 4 bytes.

An "item" is a single uniform slot. So 16 bytes. A mat4x4 is 4 items because it consumes 4 uniform slots. A float is one item since it consumes a uniform slot despite being only 4 bytes, it wastes 16 bytes in the uniform data buffer. A vec4 is also one item. 

When you enabled instance uniforms on a node. The node will reserve 16 slots which are shared by all materials on that node.

You're saying that each float consumes 16 bytes, but that contradicts the [doc](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/shading_language.html#uniform-limits), which claims that floats are not padded. Maybe it's different for instance uniforms, and the doc is not specific enough about normal uniforms vs instance uniforms?

Regarding the limit, you said that each node is allocated the space for 16 items, and each item is 16 bytes. So `16 items * 16 bytes/item  = 256 bytes per node`. In my testing, I found that 256 nodes was the max amount I was able to create before getting errors. So `256 bytes/node * 256 nodes = 65,536 bytes`, which is exactly the number listed in Project Settings as the default buffer size. It's also 64 Kibibytes, and Nvidia specs show that 64 KB is the UBO buffer size. So I guess Godot is using UBO for instance uniforms, and they've set the default buffer size to be equal to Nvidia specs?

What's weird is that the number in Project Settings does not seem to be respected on the AMD machine. 65536 was set in Project Settings and I was getting no errors there.

Also, the description in Project Settings says that the buffer size is "the maximum number of uniforms that can be used by the global shader uniform buffer". Based on what you're saying, that description is wrong. It's the number of bytes, not the number of uniforms.

> You're saying that each float consumes 16 bytes, but that contradicts the [doc](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/shading_language.html#uniform-limits), which claims that floats are not padded. Maybe it's different for instance uniforms, and the doc is not specific enough about normal uniforms vs instance uniforms?

That's right. What I said aboce is about instance uniforms, and that doc was written long before instance uniforms existed. 

> Regarding the limit, you said that each node is allocated the space for 16 items, and each item is 16 bytes. So `16 items * 16 bytes/item = 256 bytes per node`. In my testing, I found that 256 nodes was the max amount I was able to create before getting errors. So `256 bytes/node * 256 nodes = 65,536 bytes`, which is exactly the number listed in Project Settings as the default buffer size. It's also 64 Kibibytes, and Nvidia specs show that 64 KB is the UBO buffer size. So I guess Godot is using UBO for instance uniforms, and they've set the default buffer size to be equal to Nvidia specs?

That is mostly right, the 65,536 bytes just happens to be the same as the default 65,536 limit. The default buffer size is significanlty larger than the NVidia max UBO size. 

65,536 items was chosen as a reasonable number of items since it is basically 1mb. It was created before the compatibility renderer existsed. The RD renderers use an SSBO which have a minimum guaranteed size that is several mbs. 65,536 was chosen to be a value that is reasonable high for most games, but low enough that the VRAM impact would be negligible.

In the compatibility renderer I chose to use a UBO so that memory access would be fast and the API would match the other renderers 1-to-1. But UBOs don't have as large of a minimum size guaranteed by the spec. 

My gut feeling is that we should use a texture instead of a UBO eventually. But that comes with a steep performance tradeoff, so it has been hard to justify. 

> What's weird is that the number in Project Settings does not seem to be respected on the AMD machine. 65536 was set in Project Settings and I was getting no errors there.
> 
> Also, the description in Project Settings says that the buffer size is "the maximum number of uniforms that can be used by the global shader uniform buffer". Based on what you're saying, that description is wrong. It's the number of bytes, not the number of uniforms.

The project setting is the number of items. Additionally, the error you got correctly identifies that the actual limit for your device is 4096 items (despite the project setting being so much higher). 

The reason that you don't get an error on AMD is likely because you aren't hitting the limit of 65,536 items

Ok, so the non-Compatibility renderers use SSBO for the instance uniforms? And the creators of those renderers evaluated that there wasn't a huge performance hit to choosing SSBO over UBO? Then how big of a change would that be to make Compatibility match those renderers and also use SSBO for instance uniforms?

> Ok, so the non-Compatibility renderers use SSBO for the instance uniforms? And the creators of those renderers evaluated that there wasn't a huge performance hit to choosing SSBO over UBO? Then how big of a change would that be to make Compatibility match those renderers and also use SSBO for instance uniforms?

SSBOs don't exist in OpenGL 3.3 :( 

The only alternative to UBOs is to use textures as I mentioned above. Which would be a pretty big change and come with a performance hit.
Dang. Should I close this issue then?
I guess it would be good to modify the docs to include a note about the instance uniform limit and Compatibility renderer.

Beside the limitations on instance uniform buffers on some hardware there also seem to be some similar limitations on web builds as indicated by https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/112674 . Is this the same type of issue? Where running using the compatibility renderer in the editor seems to allow for a larger number of instance uniforms in use than if you run a web build of the project on the same machine?

> Beside the limitations on instance uniform buffers on some hardware there also seem to be some similar limitations on web builds as indicated by [#112674](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/112674) . Is this the same type of issue? Where running using the compatibility renderer in the editor seems to allow for a larger number of instance uniforms in use than if you run a web build of the project on the same machine?

It might be. WebGL doesn't necessarily have the same limits as desktop GL even on the same GPU. 

If it is the same issue, you would get the error reported above in the console on your web build
